0.Option: Dapsone-free alternative regimens demonstrated comparable clinical efficacy to standard MDT in multibacillary leprosy patients, despite a non-significantly longer treatment duration and slower bacterial index decline in the high-bacillary load subgroup.
0.Discussion_Source: In our study, dapsone-free alternative regimens (RFP + B663 ± clarithromycin/ofloxacin/minocycline) demonstrated comparable clinical efficacy to standard MDT in MB patients and have an overall favorable safety profile, providing a viable option for HLA-B*13:01 carriers.
Evidence: At year 2, cure rates were 20.2% (22/109) in the alternative group versus 11.6% (17/147) in MDT; and at year 5, 67.6% (46/68) versus 65.8% (77/117). No significant between-group differences were observed at any timepoint (P = 0.06 and 0.80, respectively; Fig 2a and S1 Table).
Among completed cases, mean treatment duration was 1.68 (±0.69) years (alternative, n = 111) versus 1.60 (±0.64) years (MDT, n = 148), with no significant difference (P = 0.37; Fig 2d).

In the aBI ≥ 4 stratum, the MDT group generally exhibited a higher BI reduction trend than the alternative group, reaching statistical significance particularly in the 4th year, with the decrease rates of 88.64% (MDT) versus 73.22% (alternative) (P = 0.04), albeit marginally significant (Fig 3c).

No significant difference was observed in overall DP between groups (P = 0.85, Fig 5a). By 60 months, 8.81% of alternative group patients versus 9.49% of MDT group patients had DP (risk difference [RD] = -0.68%, 95% CI [-9.04%, 7.68%]).

Over a maximum follow-up of 9 years, the relapse rates were comparable between alternative therapy (0.46/100 PY) and MB-MDT (0.20/100 PY). Poisson regression confirmed no significant difference (RR = 2.23, 95% CI: 0.37–16.95; P = 0.38).
0.Rationale: The conclusion integrates multiple key findings from the Passage Body: (1) cure rates were not significantly different between groups at multiple timepoints; (2) treatment duration was similar overall; (3) while BI decline was slower in the alternative regimen among high-bacillary-load patients, this difference was not consistent across all timepoints and did not translate into worse clinical outcomes; (4) relapse and disability progression rates were comparable. These data collectively support the inference that alternative regimens are clinically equivalent to standard MDT despite minor differences in bacteriological response. The conclusion is not explicitly stated in the Passage Body but is logically derived by synthesizing evidence across outcomes (cure, relapse, disability, BI, treatment duration) and applying epidemiological reasoning about clinical equivalence. It meets the novelty, derivability, and complexity requirements, and avoids speculation or reliance on external data.

1.Option: The west-to-east gradient in dengue outbreak timing is robust in western Indonesia but breaks down in eastern Indonesia, indicating that climate-driven seasonality patterns differ significantly across the archipelago.
1.Discussion_Source: The west-to-east gradient we observed aligns with the progression of the Australian-Asian monsoon system, which moves from northwest to southeast across the Indonesian archipelago [31]. This suggests that provincial differences in peak timing reflect climate-driven seasonality rather than sequential disease spread between provinces. The gradient was strongest when analysis was restricted to Sumatra and Java-Bali (Table 1), and weakened substantially when eastern provinces were included. This indicates that the gradient is a robust feature of western Indonesia but breaks down in the eastern archipelago.
Evidence: Western provinces, especially in Sumatra, showed earlier seasonal peaks, while eastern provinces displayed delayed patterns.

Wavelet analysis revealed a systematic west-to-east gradient in annual dengue wave timing (Fig 2A; mean with 2.5th-97.5th percentile ranges of pairwise differences are available in Fig B in S1 Appendix). Provinces in Sumatra and western Kalimantan showed negative phase lags (averaging peaks 1.4 months earlier than the national average), while Java-Bali and eastern Kalimantan (averaging peaks 0.8 months later) and eastern provinces (averaging peaks 0.1 months later) showed positive phase lags.

The west-to-east gradient, as measured by Spearman correlations, was strongest for western provinces only (Sumatra + Java-Bali; median Spearman rho = 0.7, significant across all years), weaker when Kalimantan was included, and weakest across all provinces.

Several factors may contribute to the breakdown of the west-to-east gradient in eastern Indonesia. First, climate regimes differ markedly across the archipelago. Aldrian and Susanto identified three distinct climatic regions in Indonesia: a monsoonal region covering southern Indonesia from Sumatra to Timor, a semi-monsoonal/equatorial region in northwestern Indonesia, and an anti-monsoonal region encompassing Maluku and northern Sulawesi with opposite seasonal patterns [32]. Eastern Indonesia experiences different climate drivers than western provinces, with ENSO and the Indian Ocean Dipole exerting independent, regionally heterogeneous effects on Indonesian rainfall, and the strength of these associations varies by climate region [33]. Indeed, DMI showed stronger associations with dengue incidence than ONI in Maluku and Nusa Tenggara, whereas ONI dominated in western and central regions.
1.Rationale: The Passage Body establishes that dengue outbreak timing varies systematically from west to east, with earlier peaks in Sumatra and later peaks in eastern provinces, and that this gradient is strongest in western Indonesia (Sumatra and Java-Bali) and weakens when eastern provinces are included. The Discussion interprets this pattern as reflecting climate-driven seasonality, specifically the progression of the Australian-Asian monsoon system, and attributes the breakdown of the gradient in eastern Indonesia to distinct regional climate regimes (e.g., anti-monsoonal patterns in Maluku and northern Sulawesi) and differing climate drivers (e.g., stronger influence of DMI in eastern regions). This conclusion integrates multiple pieces of evidence: the spatial pattern of phase lags, the statistical strength of the gradient across geographic subregions, and the known climatic heterogeneity across the archipelago. It is not explicitly stated in the Passage Body but is logically derived by applying epidemiological reasoning to the observed spatiotemporal patterns and known climatic drivers. The conclusion is complex, requires integration of multiple data points, and represents a key finding of the study.

2.Option: The epidemic’s trajectory, defined by a high-risk cluster strongly associated with livestock scale and modulated by lagged and immediate socioeconomic factors, reflects a systemic failure in integrating health security with economic development in pastoral regions.
2.Discussion_Source: The epidemic’s trajectory, defined by a high-risk cluster strongly associated with livestock scale and modulated by lagged and immediate socioeconomic factors, reflects a systemic failure in integrating health security with economic development in pastoral regions.
Evidence: The study was conducted in the Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region, a major pastoral area in northwestern China, with its internal administrative divisions into five prefecture-level cities shown in Fig 1a. Between 2007 and 2022, the region experienced a dramatic intensification of the human brucellosis epidemic. The overall incidence rate surged from 0.52 to 86.83 per 100,000 population, a 167-fold increase.

The most prominent was a persistent, high-risk cluster (Cluster 1), active from January 2015 to December 2022. This cluster covered 11 counties in central and eastern Ningxia and was associated with a 4.22-fold higher relative risk (RR) compared to areas outside the cluster.

The analysis identified several factors with exceptional explanatory power (q-statistic > 0.90). Sheep inventory (q = 0.963) and regional GDP (q = 0.958) emerged as the strongest individual determinants, followed closely by cattle inventory (q = 0.924) and the gross output value of animal husbandry (q = 0.936) (Table 3).

The final DLNM revealed distinct temporal patterns of association (Table 4). A significant delayed effect was observed for standardized cattle inventory. Specifically, an increase in cattle inventory was associated with a peak in relative risk (RR = 2.75, 95% CI: 1.22–6.18) at a three-year lag. For standardized sheep inventory, an increase was associated with a reduced risk at both one-year and three-year lags (RR = 0.27 and 0.08, respectively). In contrast, several factors showed immediate (lag 0) effects: increases in beef and dairy production were associated with elevated contemporaneous risk (RR = 1.25 and 1.34, respectively), whereas an increase in regional GDP exhibited a protective effect (RR = 0.81).
2.Rationale: The conclusion integrates multiple pieces of evidence from the Passage Body: (1) the emergence of a persistent, high-risk spatiotemporal cluster (RR = 4.22) in areas with intensive ruminant husbandry; (2) the quantitatively dominant role of livestock scale (sheep and cattle inventory) in explaining spatial heterogeneity (q > 0.92); and (3) the distinct temporal dynamics—delayed risk from cattle inventory (3-year lag) and immediate protective effect of GDP (lag 0). These findings, when interpreted through the lens of epidemiological systems thinking, indicate that the epidemic is not merely a result of biological transmission but is structurally embedded in the interplay between economic development (GDP) and livestock intensification, with health security lagging behind. This systemic failure is not explicitly stated in the Passage Body but is logically derivable from the integration of spatiotemporal patterns, spatial determinants, and temporal dynamics. The conclusion meets the novelty, derivability, and complexity requirements by synthesizing data across multiple analytical stages and applying general epidemiological principles to infer a structural, policy-level insight.

3.Option: The detection of Leishmania infantum DNA in a captive maned wolf within a visceral leishmaniasis–endemic urban zoo highlights the relevance of zoological institutions as critical interfaces for One Health surveillance.
3.Discussion_Source: The detection of Leishmania infantum DNA in a captive maned wolf within a visceral leishmaniasis–endemic urban zoo highlights the relevance of zoological institutions as critical interfaces for One Health surveillance.
Evidence: The Belo Horizonte Zoo (BH Zoo) is situated in a visceral leishmaniases-endemic area, raising concerns about the potential role of captive wild animals as silent hosts within the local transmission cycle.
Entomological surveillance conducted at the BH Zoo between 2019 and 2021 identified Lu. longipalpis as the predominant sand fly species, accounting for more than 65% of captured specimens.
High vector densities were recorded in enclosures housing gorillas and maned wolves, including the enclosure of the Le. infantum–positive individual identified in this study.

A total of 31 skin biopsies and 41 blood samples from wild mammals (orders Primates and Carnivora) were screened for Leishmania DNA using three complementary molecular methods: nested PCR (LnPCR), real time PCR (qPCR), and K26-loop-mediated isothermal amplification (K-26 LAMP).

Among blood samples, only one—collected from a maned wolf (Chrysocyon brachyurus; sample no. 19, ID 245565)—yielded a positive result. This sample produced the expected 358-bp amplicon in the second round of LnPCR and was also positive by K26-LAMP, as indicated by a color change from pink to yellow.

The 358-bp LnPCR amplicon obtained from the maned wolf (Chrysocyon brachyurus, sample B19) was sequenced and compared with reference sequences available in the GenBank database. BLAST analysis revealed 100% nucleotide identity with Leishmania infantum.
The sequence obtained from the maned wolf (GenBank accession PV797395) clustered robustly within the Le. infantum clade, with 100% bootstrap support.
3.Rationale: The conclusion is derived from integrating multiple pieces of evidence: (1) the study was conducted in an urban zoo located in a known visceral leishmaniasis-endemic area; (2) competent vectors (Lutzomyia longipalpis) were detected at high densities in enclosures housing susceptible species, including the maned wolf; (3) Leishmania infantum DNA was molecularly confirmed in a captive maned wolf, a species of conservation concern; and (4) the detection occurred despite the animal being clinically healthy. These findings collectively support the inference that zoos in endemic areas serve as critical interfaces where human, animal, and environmental health intersect, making them valuable sites for One Health surveillance. This conclusion is not explicitly stated in the Passage Body but is logically derived from the integration of epidemiological, ecological, and molecular evidence, and aligns with the broader One Health framework introduced in the Passage Body.

4.Option: Despite possessing basic awareness of modern first-aid principles, a considerable proportion of Public Health Midwives in Sri Lanka endorse harmful traditional practices such as sucking venom, applying herbs, or cutting the bite site, indicating a gap between theoretical knowledge and actual practices.
4.Discussion_Source: Findings reveal that while most PHMs possessed basic awareness of the importance of early hospital transfer and the need to reassure and immobilize the patient, a considerable proportion endorsed harmful traditional practices such as sucking venom, applying herbs, or cutting the bite site. These findings underscore a critical gap between correct knowledge and actual beliefs that could influence field practices, particularly in rural areas where PHMs serve as primary sources of emergency advice.
Evidence: Most PHMs correctly recognised the importance of reassuring and calming the victim (95.9%) and transporting the child promptly to a hospital with antivenom facilities (95.8%).

However, widespread endorsement of traditional and potentially harmful practices was observed. A majority indicated that they would suck out the venom (71.6%), apply herbs (73.2%), or make an incision at the bite site (64.4%).
4.Rationale: The Passage Body shows that PHMs have high awareness of recommended first-aid actions (e.g., reassurance, prompt transport), but also reports that a large majority endorse harmful practices (e.g., sucking venom, cutting, applying herbs). This contrast between correct theoretical knowledge and endorsement of dangerous practices constitutes a clear gap. The conclusion is derived by integrating two distinct pieces of evidence: one confirming correct knowledge and another showing endorsement of harmful actions. This gap is not explicitly stated in the Passage Body but is logically inferable through epidemiological reasoning about the distinction between knowledge and behavior, particularly in the context of public health interventions. The conclusion meets the novelty, derivability, and complexity requirements, as it synthesizes multiple data points and reflects a key insight beyond simple reporting.

5.Option: The lower seroprevalence of rickettsial infections observed in blood donors compared to previous reports in febrile patients may be due to selection bias, as blood donors are less likely to have been exposed to rickettsial vectors and may represent a healthier, more urbanized population with different exposure patterns.
5.Discussion_Source: This study demonstrates substantial prior exposure to both STG and TG in multiple provinces of Laos, including during the COVID-19 period. However, these findings reflect past exposure in healthy individuals and do not directly quantify the current burden of febrile illness attributable to rickettsia infections.
Evidence: The study population was stratified into five age groups (17–24, 25–30, 31–36, 37–46, and ≥47 years). These categories were selected to capture distinct life stages, ranging from late adolescence and young adulthood to mid-life and older adulthood. The chosen ranges also ensured adequate sample sizes in each group, enabling robust statistical analysis while maintaining relevance to sociocultural and occupational transitions that may influence exposure risk.

Most blood donors are younger adults and random sampling was not possible. Selection of samples for this study was based on donor age and sample availability, to be representative of different age groups.

In the current study, STG and TG were detected in only 1% and 2% of participants, respectively. Several factors may explain the conflicting findings between this study and previous reports, including that blood donors may not represent the general population, as they are less exposed to reservoirs or vectors, have limited age diversity, and differ in exposure-related behaviors.

We did not collect detailed data on socioeconomic status, education level, occupation, or residential classification, these factors may influence differences in seropositivity between febrile patients and blood donors.
In addition, residential classification (urban versus rural) was not systematically recorded for donors in the present study, limiting direct comparison of exposure setting with the previous report.

One possible explanation is that sample collection occurred during the COVID-19 pandemic, with blood collection between January and August 2021. During this period, tighter movement restrictions were implemented in April 2021 which may have temporarily influenced population mobility and short-term exposure.

However, IgG antibodies can persist for at least 18 months in scrub typhus patients [16] and up to 12 months in murine typhus patients [9], showing higher antibody levels due to recent immune activation. In contrast, blood donors represent individuals with past exposure resulting in lower IgG titers.
5.Rationale: The conclusion integrates multiple pieces of evidence from the Passage Body: (1) blood donors are predominantly younger adults with limited age diversity; (2) selection was based on availability and age, not random sampling; (3) donors are likely less exposed to vectors due to occupational and residential patterns; (4) the study was conducted during a period of movement restrictions; and (5) IgG persistence suggests that donors represent past, not recent, exposure. These factors collectively support the inference that blood donors are not representative of the general population in terms of rickettsial exposure, leading to lower seroprevalence compared to febrile patients. This conclusion is not explicitly stated in the Passage Body but is logically derived from the methodological limitations and demographic characteristics described, and it reflects a key epidemiological insight about selection bias in seroprevalence studies using non-representative populations.

6.Option: Without appropriate adaptation of public health strategies, declining T. gondii exposure may increase susceptibility among women of reproductive age, particularly in populations undergoing rapid urbanization or socioeconomic transition, or rapid increases in temperature.
6.Discussion_Source: Without appropriate adaptation of public health strategies, declining T. gondii exposure may increase susceptibility among women of reproductive age, particularly in populations undergoing rapid urbanization or socioeconomic transition, or rapid increases in temperature.
Evidence: The large majority of cases of congenital toxoplasmosis occur in women experiencing their first infection during pregnancy [6], although cases in women following infection with a different serotype, or resurgence in immunosuppressed mothers have also been reported [7].

As described for rubella [8], if the force of infection is very high, most individuals will be infected for the first time early in life, and thus will not be at risk during pregnancy; if the force of infection is very low, very few individuals will be infected at all, and thus the burden will be low. Intermediate levels of the force of infection may thus convey the greatest burden within a population (Fig 2).

Our results align with expectations: risk declines with HDI and maximum temperature - and also enable us to explore future burden under projections of demographic change across a range of temperature changes.

Combining these results with estimates of current and future births across age ... we find a vast diversity of outcomes, ranging from halving to near doubling of the burden of congenital toxoplasmosis (Fig 5).

An increase in maximum temperature in general decreases the burden of congenital toxoplasmosis, while effects of increases in the minimum temperature or both minimum and maximum temperature are variable.
6.Rationale: The Passage Body establishes that congenital toxoplasmosis risk is highest when women experience a primary infection during pregnancy, and that the force of infection (FOI) determines the age at first infection. It further shows that FOI declines with higher HDI and maximum temperature, and that intermediate FOI levels lead to the highest burden due to a 'paradoxical' effect: if FOI is too high, most people are infected early and not at risk during pregnancy; if FOI is too low, few are infected at all. The analysis projects that rising temperatures (especially maximum temperature) reduce FOI and thus burden, but demographic changes (e.g., delayed childbearing) can shift risk. The Discussion synthesizes this by stating that declining exposure (due to higher temperature or improved HDI) may increase susceptibility in reproductive-age women, especially in transitioning populations—this is a logical inference from the FOI-burden relationship and the projected decline in FOI under climate change. This conclusion is not explicitly stated in the Passage Body but is derivable from the interplay of FOI, age at infection, demographic shifts, and temperature effects, and requires integrating multiple pieces of evidence and applying epidemiological principles of risk dynamics.

7.Option: rTsSPc immunization significantly reduced intestinal goblet cell hyperplasia and mucus overproduction by preventing parasite-induced intestinal barrier damage and suppressing pathological inflammatory responses.
7.Discussion_Source: In the infected PBS group, T. spiralis infection and sustained stimulation of the worms-secreted TsSPc led to intestinal injury and inflammation. To counteract this damage, host initiated the marked inflammatory cell infiltration, excessive goblet cell hyperplasia, and plentiful of mucus secretion. The increased number of goblet cells observed in infected PBS group is really a state of intestinal pathological stress and hyper-responsiveness. ... In this study, obvious reduction of goblet cells in rTsSPc+infection group serves as a direct evidence that intestinal pathological injury has been successfully prevented or markedly alleviated, and constitutes a robust demonstration of the vaccine’s protective efficacy.
Evidence: In infected PBS and ISA201 groups, goblet cell number was significantly increased with enlarged volume, and Muc2/Muc5ac transcription levels were significantly higher than the rTsSPc-immunized group at one week post infection.
The increased number of goblet cells observed in infected PBS group is really a state of intestinal pathological stress and hyper-responsiveness.

In this study, obvious reduction of goblet cells in rTsSPc+infection group serves as a direct evidence that intestinal pathological injury has been successfully prevented or markedly alleviated, and constitutes a robust demonstration of the vaccine’s protective efficacy.
7.Rationale: The Passage Body shows that in infected control mice (PBS and ISA201 groups), there is a significant increase in goblet cell number and mucus production (Muc2/Muc5ac) following T. spiralis infection, which is interpreted as a pathological stress response to intestinal barrier damage. In contrast, rTsSPc-immunized mice show a significant reduction in goblet cell numbers and mucus levels. The Discussion explicitly links this reduction to the prevention of intestinal injury and suppression of pathological inflammation, which are consequences of the vaccine's ability to neutralize TsSPc and preserve intestinal integrity. This conclusion integrates multiple pieces of evidence: histopathological findings (goblet cell count), molecular data (mucin gene expression), and immunological mechanisms (antibody-mediated neutralization of TsSPc). It is not a direct numerical summary, does not merely describe a limitation or future direction, and is not a generic statement. It is a novel inference derived from the data using standard immunological and pathological reasoning, making it a strong candidate for a correct reasoning test option.

8.Option: The AI-DP platform enables near-real-time, quality-assured data while reducing the burden on technicians, which supports improved efficiency in STH and intestinal SCH control programs within endemic, resource-constrained settings.
8.Discussion_Source: The AI-DP platform enables near-real-time, quality-assured data while reducing the burden on technicians, which supports improved efficiency in STH and intestinal SCH control programs within endemic, resource-constrained settings.
Evidence: By integrating WSI scanners, onboard AI analysis, and human-in-the-loop verification, it provides near-real-time, quality-assured data while reducing the burden on technicians.
Automation frees technicians for parallel tasks, promising substantial labour savings – critical given that personnel costs constitute 42–74% of M&E survey expenses [9].

In addition to efficiency gains, the AI-DP platform offers operational advantages over human-only microscopy workflows. AI-DP detection is not affected by operator fatigue in the same way as human microscopists, whose accuracy and thoroughness can decline over long reading sessions.
These factors can enhance reproducibility and reliability of results across time, sites, and operators.
8.Rationale: The conclusion integrates multiple pieces of evidence from the Passage Body: (1) the platform uses AI and human-in-the-loop verification to generate near-real-time data; (2) it reduces technician burden by automating detection and freeing staff for parallel tasks; (3) it mitigates operator fatigue, ensuring consistent performance; and (4) it improves reproducibility across settings. These points, when combined with the known high personnel costs (42–74% of expenses), allow for the logical inference that the platform enhances program efficiency in resource-constrained, endemic areas. This conclusion is not explicitly stated in the Passage Body but is derivable through epidemiological reasoning about operational efficiency, cost, and workforce sustainability in public health monitoring programs.

9.Option: The inflammatory profile in R. aegyptiacus cells more closely resembled that of non-reservoir mammalian hosts than the immune-tolerant responses observed in established bat-virus reservoir systems, suggesting that ZIKV is unlikely to be a well-adapted virus in this species.
9.Discussion_Source: The inflammatory profile in R. aegyptiacus cells more closely resembled that of non-reservoir mammalian hosts than the immune-tolerant responses observed in established bat-virus reservoir systems, suggesting that ZIKV is unlikely to be a well-adapted virus in this species.
Evidence: R06E cells supported productive replication of both African (ZIKV/MR766) and Asian-American (ZIKV/PRVABC59) lineage ZIKV isolates (Fig 1A), indicating that R. aegyptiacus cells are permissive to ZIKV infection.

Both African (ZIKV/MR766) and Asian-American (ZIKV/PRVABC59) isolates triggered robust antiviral and pro-inflammatory responses in R06E cells. Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) of R06E cells revealed upregulation of immune-related pathways at 6 HPI, including “viral protein interaction with cytokine and cytokine receptor”, “toll-like receptor signaling,” and “rheumatoid arthritis” (Fig 2A, 2B).
These pathways are commonly associated with innate immune activation against viral infections, particularly those driven by interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs).
Although we hypothesized that R. aegyptiacus might exhibit a similarly immune tolerant profile following ZIKV infection, our findings instead reveal a more complex and context-dependent pattern.

The observed transcriptional responses in R06E cells are consistent with literature on ZIKV infection in other mammals, namely humans and primates, rather than the immune tolerant phenotype observed in R06E cells following infection with MARV [53] (Fig 6).

Previous findings from Viet et al. show that flavivirus NS5 proteins—particularly from ZIKV—partially antagonize STAT2-dependent signaling, including in various bat taxa [56]. While our transcriptomic analysis of R06E cells revealed robust upregulation of ISGs, including OAS3, MX2, and DDX58, we found that R06E cells supported robust replication of ZIKV.
9.Rationale: The conclusion is derived from integrating multiple lines of evidence from the Passage Body: (1) R. aegyptiacus cells (R06E) support productive ZIKV replication; (2) they mount a robust pro-inflammatory and antiviral transcriptional response, including upregulation of ISGs and cytokine-related pathways; (3) this response resembles that seen in non-reservoir mammals (e.g., humans and primates) rather than the immune-tolerant responses seen in other bat-virus systems (e.g., Marburg virus in R. aegyptiacus); and (4) despite evidence of STAT2 antagonism by ZIKV NS5, ISG upregulation persists, indicating a non-canonical or incomplete immune evasion. The inference that ZIKV is not well-adapted to R. aegyptiacus—meaning it does not induce a balanced, tolerant immune response typical of long-term reservoir hosts—is logically supported by the absence of immune tolerance and the presence of strong inflammatory activation. This conclusion is not explicitly stated in the Passage Body but is a direct inference from the described immune response patterns and their contrast with known reservoir systems.

10.Option: The disconnect between knowledge and action among abattoir workers underscores the need for targeted, context-sensitive interventions beyond awareness campaigns to address structural and behavioural barriers to safe practices.
10.Discussion_Source: These findings suggest that awareness alone cannot change behaviour and that knowledge does not necessarily drive practices. This disconnect between knowledge and action underscores the need for targeted, context-sensitive interventions beyond awareness campaigns to address structural and behavioural barriers to safe practices.
Evidence: Although a general awareness of zoonotic transmission was reported in several studies, this awareness rarely translated into consistent protective behaviour.

Unsafe practices, such as non-use of personal protective equipment (PPE), consumption of raw meat or milk, poor hand hygiene, and improper carcass and waste handling, were common despite some knowledge of the risks involved.

In one study, participants identified food sellers, butchers, and herders as high-risk groups due to their frequent contact with raw animal products, reflecting an understanding of occupational exposure risks [28]. Another study highlighted that while workers recognised the importance of using PPE and handwashing after handling animal body fluids, this recognition was not always reflected in their routine practices [19].
10.Rationale: The Passage Body provides evidence that abattoir workers possess varying levels of knowledge about zoonotic disease transmission (e.g., 83% knew leptospirosis could be transmitted from animals to humans, but only 31% recognized the zoonotic potential of bovine tuberculosis). However, despite this knowledge, unsafe practices such as non-use of PPE, consumption of raw meat, and poor hygiene were consistently reported. The Discussion explicitly interprets this as a 'disconnect between knowledge and action,' which is not directly stated in the Passage Body. This conclusion is derivable through epidemiological reasoning: the persistence of high-risk behaviours in the presence of partial knowledge indicates that knowledge alone is insufficient to drive behaviour change. The need for interventions that go beyond awareness—addressing structural (e.g., lack of PPE) and behavioural (e.g., cultural norms, perceived invulnerability) barriers—is a logical inference from the evidence. The conclusion meets all requirements: it is novel (not stated in the Passage Body), derivable from the data, complex (integrates knowledge, attitudes, and practices), and not speculative or generic.

11.Option: The genomic evidence indicates that dengue transmission in southern Brazil is not sporadic or incidental but instead embedded within broader national transmission networks.
11.Discussion_Source: The genomic evidence presented here indicates that dengue transmission in this region is not sporadic or incidental but instead embedded within broader national transmission networks.
Evidence: All DENV-1 genomes were classified as Genotype V (lineages E.1 and D.1.1) and all DENV-2 genomes as Genotype II (lineage F.1.1.2), both previously reported in Brazil [13,14].
DENV-1 was widely distributed across Porto Alegre’s five macro-regions, while DENV-2 was geographically limited to the East and Northeast zones (Fig 1a).

Phylogenetic analysis revealed that DENV-1 sequences from this study clustered into four distinct clades (Fig 1b). Most grouped with sequences from southern Brazil, consistent with ongoing local transmission, while others clustered with viruses from different regions, suggesting multiple introductions and regional viral exchange.
DENV-2 sequences were nested among those previously sampled from the South, preceding the 2024 outbreak across southern and southeastern Brazil (Fig 1c).
11.Rationale: The Passage Body provides multiple lines of evidence: (1) the detection of DENV-1 and DENV-2 in mosquito pools across multiple urban zones in Porto Alegre; (2) the phylogenetic clustering of DENV-1 sequences with both local and non-local Brazilian strains, indicating regional viral exchange; (3) the presence of DENV-2 sequences nested within previously sampled South Brazilian viruses; and (4) the classification of both serotypes as genotypes already established in Brazil. Together, these data demonstrate that the viruses detected in southern Brazil are not isolated or novel introductions but are part of a continuous transmission network across the country. This conclusion is not explicitly stated in the Passage Body but is logically derived by integrating spatial distribution, phylogenetic relationships, and known genotypic patterns using standard epidemiological and phylogeographic reasoning. The conclusion meets the novelty, derivability, and complexity requirements, as it synthesizes multiple findings to infer a systemic transmission pattern rather than a single observation.

12.Option: The persistent expansion of built-up areas in Goa, driven by rapid urbanization and construction activities, has created ecological conditions conducive to sustained Aedes mosquito breeding and dengue transmission in urban and peri-urban regions.
12.Discussion_Source: The continuous expansion of the construction and hospitality sectors to sustain tourism has attracted scores of migrant workers from different parts of India to Goa. The malaria outbreaks in Goa are largely attributed to these migrant workers, who carry the Plasmodium parasites from malaria-endemic states [39]. It is plausible that these migrant workers from across India could have facilitated the spread of different dengue serotypes across Goa. A substantial proportion of dengue infections in India are asymptomatic, contributing to a large hidden pool of transmission. A community-based study showed asymptomatic dengue cases outnumbered clinical cases, and serological surveys revealed that subclinical infections comprised 40% of all dengue cases in Delhi [9,40]. According to the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control, 40–80% of all dengue infections are asymptomatic, acting as a reservoir for silent transmission [41]. This is compounded by severe underreporting in India; only 0.35% of clinically diagnosed dengue cases are captured in national surveillance, and the actual burden is extremely higher than official figures [42]. The influx of migrant workers from hyperendemic regions with asymptomatic and viremic strains, coupled with ongoing construction-driven proliferation of Aedes aegypti in urban centers of Goa, could have facilitated dengue transmission (symptomatic and asymptomatic) to the naive local population. Hidden asymptomatic infections complicate disease surveillance and may increase the likelihood of severe infections when re-infected with heterologous serotypes. Therefore, integrated serological and molecular surveillance systems, extending beyond febrile cases, are crucial for detecting and mitigating these silent transmission chains, especially in urban clusters reporting dengue outbreaks.
Evidence: In addition to built-up area, pits and barren lands (labelled as misc in Fig 8 have also increased by replacing the scrub lands. The health centers that reported high dengue cases were situated in the highly built-up areas, and their surroundings, especially in coastal regions.
The four urban health centers in the state—Mapusa, Panaji, Vasco, and Margao continuously report high caseloads and account for 30.48% of all the dengue cases reported since 2011.
The health centers that reported high dengue cases were situated in the highly built-up areas, and their surroundings, especially in coastal regions.
The continuous expansion of the construction and hospitality sectors to sustain tourism has attracted scores of migrant workers from different parts of India to Goa.

The influx of migrant workers from hyperendemic regions with asymptomatic and viremic strains, coupled with ongoing construction-driven proliferation of Aedes aegypti in urban centers of Goa, could have facilitated dengue transmission (symptomatic and asymptomatic) to the naive local population.

The primary dengue vector, Aedes aegypti, is widespread across Goa [13,32,33]. Its ability to breed in small man-made containers, resistance to overcrowding, and tolerance to large temperature ranges make it highly adapted to breeding in urban households [34] and have enabled it to out-compete An. stephensi in many settings [35,36]. ID02 (D. albiventris) harbored both T. cruzi, detected in blood and lymph node samples, and T. lainsoni, identified by parasitological culture of blood and PCR from a tail skin fragment. ID09 (N. squamipes) was co-infected with L. infantum, detected through xenodiagnoses followed by PCR of fed sand flies, and T. lainsoni, isolated from blood culture.
The proximity of MT to neighboring residential areas facilitates interactions between humans, domestic animals, and wildlife across natural and urbanized interfaces.

The study area has previously reported autochthonous cases of canine visceral leishmaniasis (Health Department of Minas Gerais), and phlebotomine sand flies carrying Leishmania DNA have also been recorded [14]. In addition, Panstrongylus megistus, one of the primary vectors of Chagas disease in Brazil, is also present in the area, supporting the plausibility of enzootic transmission cycles in the area [15,16].
26.Rationale: The conclusion integrates multiple pieces of evidence from the Passage Body: (1) the presence of zoonotic trypanosomatids (L. infantum, L. braziliensis, T. cruzi, T. lainsoni) in small mammals; (2) the detection of these pathogens in multiple hosts across species; (3) the presence of competent vectors (L. longipalpis, P. megistus) and prior reports of human/animal cases in the region; and (4) the ecological context of a fragmented peri-urban forest with high human-wildlife contact. While the Discussion explicitly states that reservoir competence and sustained transmission cannot be confirmed due to limitations, the Passage Body provides sufficient evidence—through direct detection of pathogens in hosts, presence of vectors, and ecological setting—to infer that these small mammals are exposed to and can harbor pathogens of public health relevance. This inference is derived via standard epidemiological reasoning: the co-occurrence of pathogen, host, and vector in a high-contact interface implies potential for transmission, even without definitive proof of sustained cycles. The conclusion is novel (not directly stated in the Results), derivable from the evidence, and meets the complexity requirement by integrating multiple lines of evidence across species, diagnostics, and ecological context.

27.Option: Wind speed appears to be a key factor determining the dispersal capacity of infected T. vitticeps in the Espírito Santo, representing a potential novel mechanism for the long-distance transmission of T. cruzi.
27.Discussion_Source: Wind speed appears to be a key factor determining the dispersal capacity of infected T. vitticeps in the Espírito Santo, representing a potential novel mechanism for the long-distance transmission of T. cruzi.
Evidence: The decision tree models reached a maximum accuracy of 62% (Fig 7 and Tables 4 and 5), reflecting the difficulty of classifying triatomines by T. cruzi infection, likely due to limitations in the temporal and spatial resolution of climatic and environmental data, as infected and uninfected vectors share habitats [99,100].

Wind has been identified as one of the factors influencing the flight displacement of triatomines, typically associated with low wind speeds and other factors such as temperature, humidity, and nutritional status [29,80,101–105].

The prevalence of winged adults and the absence of nymphs reinforce this idea, suggesting that the flight capacity of T. vitticeps, likely enhanced by the mountainous relief and prevailing air currents of the Central mesoregion, facilitates long-distance dispersal, supporting Dario et al.’s hypothesis [10,11,41].

Thus, wind speed appears to be a key factor determining the dispersal capacity of infected T. vitticeps in the Espírito Santo, representing a potential novel mechanism for the long-distance transmission of T. cruzi.
27.Rationale: The Passage Body establishes that T. vitticeps is a wild species that invades houses, particularly in mountainous regions, and that its flight capacity is enhanced by mountainous terrain and air currents. It also notes that winged adults are prevalent and nymphs are absent, suggesting active dispersal. The decision tree analysis identified wind speed as a key variable in classifying infected triatomines. By integrating these observations—flight capability, environmental context (mountainous terrain), and wind as a predictor in the model—epidemiological reasoning supports the conclusion that wind speed is a critical driver of long-distance dispersal. This conclusion is not explicitly stated in the Passage Body but is logically derived from the combination of ecological, spatial, and modeling evidence. It meets the novelty requirement because the idea of wind-driven long-distance transmission is not directly asserted in the results, and it satisfies derivability by relying only on data and principles within the Passage Body (e.g., flight behavior, terrain, and model outputs). The conclusion is complex, integrating multiple data streams and representing a key insight into transmission dynamics.

28.Option: The detection of Colpodella spp. in Hyalomma anatolicum ticks highlights the need for further investigation into the vector competence of ticks and the possible zoonotic transmission of this pathogen.
28.Discussion_Source: The detection of Colpodella spp. in Hyalomma anatolicum ticks highlights the need for further investigation into the vector competence of ticks and the possible zoonotic transmission of this pathogen.
Evidence: Molecular screening revealed the presence of multiple tick-borne pathogens, with Colpodella spp. being the most frequently detected. This protozoan was primarily found in Hy. excavatum collected from Buner and Kohistan, with prevalence rates of 8.98% (15/167) and 5.48% (9/164), respectively (Table 3). In Chitral, Colpodella spp. was also detected in Hy. anatolicum, where 8 of 100 ticks tested positive (8%).

Colpodella spp., a free-living microorganism closely related to apicomplexan parasites, represents an evolutionary bridge between free-living protozoa and parasitic apicomplexans [27,28,18]. More recently, Colpodella spp. have been reported to infect vertebrates (e.g., Amur tiger, horse) and humans, which are thought to possibly be transmitted by infected Rhipicephalus microplus, Dermacentor everestianus, and D. nuttalli ticks [29,30,31]. Although little is currently known about the pathogenicity, vectoral capacity, and geographical distribution of Colpodella spp., they may pose an under-recognized public health risk [32,33].

The phylogenetic analysis revealed that the Colpodella spp. sequence from this study showed 100% identity with a sequence isolated from Rh. haemaphysaloides in China and 99.92% with a sequence from a woman in China with relapsing Babesia-like illness.
28.Rationale: The Passage Body establishes that Colpodella spp. was detected in Hyalomma anatolicum ticks in Chitral (8/100, 8%), and that this pathogen has previously been linked to human infections via tick bites in China. The phylogenetic analysis confirms high sequence identity between the detected pathogen and a strain isolated from a human with a Babesia-like illness. This evidence supports the inference that the presence of Colpodella spp. in Hy. anatolicum—especially in a region where human infections have been documented—raises concerns about potential zoonotic transmission. The conclusion is not explicitly stated in the Passage Body but is logically derived by integrating the detection of the pathogen in a tick species, its known association with vertebrate and human infections, and its genetic similarity to a human-pathogenic strain. The conclusion meets the novelty, derivability, and complexity requirements by synthesizing data across multiple sections (Results, Background, and Phylogenetic Analysis) and applying epidemiological reasoning about vector competence and zoonotic risk.

29.Option: Although normalization of heart rate variability parameters was observed after benznidazole treatment, a reduced inhibitory response of the parasympathetic branch persisted 8 months post-treatment, as indicated by altered heart rate recovery during the exercise stress test.
29.Discussion_Source: This study demonstrated a tendency towards sympathovagal imbalance and a reduced inhibitory response of the parasympathetic branch in the acute phase. The 5-minute HRV analysis showed no statistically significant changes in the indices.

Heart Rate Recovery (HRR) was observed to show an altered response and statistical significance (p = 0.006; d = 1.05). This index is associated with an inhibition of the parasympathetic response.
