Since HRR is a well-established marker of parasympathetic function, this finding indicates that despite global normalization of HRV, a specific deficit in parasympathetic inhibitory control persisted. This conclusion integrates two pieces of evidence: the general normalization of HRV and the specific persistence of abnormal HRR. It is not explicitly stated in the Passage Body but is logically derivable through standard epidemiological and physiological reasoning about autonomic function assessment. The conclusion meets the novelty, derivability, and complexity requirements, as it requires synthesizing data across multiple assessment methods (HRV and exercise stress test) and interpreting a nuanced clinical finding.

30.Option: The classification of ENL as acute, recurrent, or chronic is inconsistent across studies, with overlapping definitions and ambiguous terminology, particularly regarding the meaning of 'episode' and the distinction between recurrence and flaring during treatment.
30.Discussion_Source: The classification of leprosy reactions has often been challenging for leprologists. In 1949 de Souza Lima [59] expressed dissatisfaction with the prevailing classification of leprosy reactions and highlighted the need to establish clear definitions agreed by the international leprosy community. This sentiment was echoed by Pettit and Waters [60], who shared the view that ENL represented an acute exacerbation of the chronic disease of leprosy. In the early period of sulfone use for leprosy treatment, some researchers hypothesised that ENL was an adverse effect of therapy [61]. Others interpreted ENL as an indicator of a favourable response [62]. However, as Pettit and Waters highlighted and we have shown, the literature prior to the introduction of sulfone anti-microbial therapy is replete with descriptions of ENL [60]. The nodular form of leprosy described by Hansen and Looft was complicated by ENL, and the affected individual eventually succumbed. As Vollset describes in his translation from Hansen and Looft: “Intermittently all affections [fever and nodules] could spontaneously disappear and the patient would heal, but in general the life of the patient would end after eight or nine years” [47] In the WHO multi-drug therapy (MDT) era, ENL occurs before, during, or after the completion of treatment [13]. It is hypothesised that bactericidal action of MDT in individuals with high bacillary load results in Mycobacterium leprae antigens inducing immune activation leading to an inflammatory response [63]. The pathophysiology of ENL is not well understood, there is evidence that pro-inflammatory cytokines such as tumour necrosis factor alfa, interferon gamma and interleukins 1 and 6 may be increased [5], all of which may contribute to ENL severity [64]. It is unclear whether immunosuppressive therapy influences the duration or type of ENL. Individuals may require corticosteroids for prolonged periods and some experience tachyphylaxis [12,22]. The reported duration of ENL “episodes” (in individuals prescribed ENL treatment) ranges from 3 to 72 days [2,3,55]. However, this may not reflect the length of exposure to high dose corticosteroids for those who have multiple episodes. The prolonged duration of treatment for chronic ENL is associated with morbidity and mortality [20,21]. Corticosteroids are the recommended first-choice treatment for patients with ENL [12]. The influence of treatment on the natural history of ENL is uncertain. Corticosteroids are not considered disease-modifying agents in other inflammatory conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis [65,66]. Whilst they provide rapid symptomatic relief, their role in altering the underlying disease trajectory is limited and generally reserved for short-term “bridging” therapy [65]. Identifying a disease modifying agent for ENL that would shorten the period individuals experience symptoms would be a significant advance in management. We have identified definitions of the natural history of ENL and their relative frequencies in the literature. We have identified weaknesses in all current definitions and suggested improvements. The current lack of standardised terminology hinders data comparison, meta-analyses, and clinical guideline development. To address the current inconsistencies, the Delphi technique [67] offers a structured method for achieving expert consensus. Observational prospective studies and analysis of routine data of individuals who decline ENL treatment would enable validation and refinement of proposed definitions, ensuring they are both evidence-based and clinically meaningful. A clear standardised clinical ENL classification is vital to improving our understanding of ENL and improving the lives of those affected by this condition.
Evidence: The six-month criterion distinguishing acute and chronic ENL is used in all current definitions. However, definitions of recurrent and chronic ENL overlap substantially, with both categories referring to multiple or prolonged episodes following initial treatment.

The definitions of recurrent ENL are based on the length of treatment free intervals between episodes which range from 15 days to 84 days (or 3 months) except for Mishra et al. [51] who defined recurrent ENL as occurrence of four to seven episodes per year, with or without treatment. Mishra’s definition introduces some overlap with chronic ENL as it includes individuals on treatment for ENL.

Chronic ENL is defined by most as exhibiting continuous or near-continuous symptoms requiring treatment for more than 6 months. Two definitions allowed treatment-free interval. Walker et al.[20] used a period without treatment of 27 days or fewer to define the same episode of chronic ENL whereas Kar et al.[50] defined the treatment-free period as less than 3 months.

The term “episode” which occurs in multiple definitions is not clearly defined. Pocaterra et al. described the end of an ENL episode when “steroid tapering ended”. Walker [20] defined an ENL episode as the occurrence requiring the institution or change of treatment; however, de Barros subsequently defined “flare” as a symptomatic exacerbation of ENL [25]. The overlap between the terms “episode” and “flare” highlights continued ambiguity in ENL terminology.

The recurrence of ENL following remission, or deterioration as treatment is reduced (“flare”) is a particularly challenging aspect of the condition. High rates of “recurrence” and/or “flaring” of ENL are reported. In India, 64.3% of individuals had “recurrent” episodes [32] as did a similar proportion in Ethiopia (63%) [58]. Kumar et al. argued that recurrence of a reactional episode within 6 weeks is due to inadequate anti-reaction treatment [32] it is unclear how one could differentiate between sub-optimal treatment of recurrent ENL from chronic ENL.
30.Rationale: The conclusion is derived from multiple pieces of evidence in the Passage Body that collectively demonstrate inconsistency in ENL classification. The evidence shows that definitions of acute, recurrent, and chronic ENL overlap significantly—especially between recurrent and chronic forms—due to differing criteria for treatment-free intervals (ranging from 15 days to 3 months). Furthermore, the term 'episode' is inconsistently defined across studies (e.g., ending with steroid tapering vs. requiring treatment change), and the distinction between recurrence (after treatment cessation) and flaring (during treatment) is blurred. These inconsistencies are not merely minor variations but represent fundamental ambiguities in terminology that hinder clinical and research comparability. The conclusion integrates these multiple points of evidence and applies general epidemiological reasoning about the importance of standardized definitions for valid data synthesis and clinical decision-making. It is not explicitly stated in the Passage Body but is logically inferable from the described inconsistencies.

31.Option: Tuberculosis emerged as the leading corticosteroid-associated cause of mortality, underscoring the need to exclude active tuberculosis prior to corticosteroid initiation and be vigilant for the reactivation of latent disease.
31.Discussion_Source: Tuberculosis emerged as the leading corticosteroid-associated cause of mortality, underscoring the need to exclude active tuberculosis prior to corticosteroid initiation and be vigilant for the reactivation of latent disease.
Evidence: Infections accounted for 76.5% of cases, including 23.1% due to Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
Tuberculosis was a significant complication, responsible for almost 10% of infections in case reports, 7.9% in prospective cohorts and nearly a quarter of reported fatalities (Table 4).
Cases typically occurred in individuals on high-dose or prolonged corticosteroid therapy. The onset varied from 2 months to over a year after corticosteroid initiation [72].
31.Rationale: The Passage Body provides multiple lines of evidence: (1) tuberculosis was the most common cause of infection-related deaths (23.1% of all corticosteroid-associated deaths), (2) it accounted for nearly a quarter of all reported fatalities, and (3) it occurred in individuals on high-dose or prolonged corticosteroid therapy. These data, when combined with the general epidemiological principle that corticosteroids suppress cell-mediated immunity and increase the risk of reactivation of latent infections like tuberculosis, allow the logical inference that tuberculosis is the leading cause of corticosteroid-associated mortality in this population. This conclusion is not explicitly stated in the Passage Body but is directly supported by the data and standard immunological reasoning. It is also novel (not stated elsewhere in the Passage Body) and complex, requiring integration of mortality data, infection patterns, and biological plausibility.

32.Option: The use of single dose azithromycin led to good healing rates among cases, a finding that supports the ongoing use of a single dose azithromycin in yaws elimination programmes.
32.Discussion_Source: The use of single dose azithromycin led to good healing rates among cases, a finding that supports the ongoing use of a single dose azithromycin in yaws elimination programmes.
Evidence: Thirty seven of the 46 (80.4%, 95% CI: 73.9–95.5%) participants had completely healed lesions.
All post treatment assessments were undertaken 4 weeks after administration of single dose oral azithromycin.
Out of the participants not completely healed, the highest number was from the HD only group (5/9; 56%), with all having painful ulcers.
At week 4 follow, samples from all the non-healed lesions were PCR negative for HD and TP.

The uniform healing by day 15 (97.3%) across all groups supports the WHO’s Morges strategy of using azithromycin MDA for yaws eradication, as it appears effective across all the aetiological agents in this setting.
32.Rationale: The Passage Body provides multiple pieces of evidence: (1) 80.4% of participants achieved complete healing at 4 weeks post-treatment; (2) all non-healed lesions tested PCR-negative for both T. pallidum and H. ducreyi, indicating no active infection; (3) healing was rapid and consistent across all aetiological groups, including HD-only cases; and (4) the study’s conclusion aligns with the WHO’s Morges Strategy. By applying standard epidemiological reasoning—interpreting treatment success rates, ruling out persistent infection, and assessing consistency across pathogen groups—the conclusion that single-dose azithromycin is effective and supports ongoing eradication efforts is logically derived. This conclusion is not explicitly stated in the Passage Body but is a direct inference from the healing data and molecular confirmation of clearance, satisfying the novelty, derivability, and complexity requirements.

33.Option: The combination of sTM and SOFA score provides superior predictive ability for 28-day mortality in HFRS patients compared to either marker alone.
33.Discussion_Source: And when the serum sTM concentration and the SOFA score are combined, their predictive ability for the mortality of HFRS patients (with an AUC of 0.9492) even exceeds that of either sTM or SOFA alone.
Evidence: The area under the curve (AUC) of sTM (Area = 0.9317) and SOFA (Area = 0.9309) both exceeded 0.93, ranking in the first tier and being significantly higher than those of traditional inflammatory, blood cell count, and coagulation indicators.
Additionally, the combination of sTM and SOFA score yielded an AUC of 0.9492, surpassing that of sTM and SOFA alone (Fig 3C).
33.Rationale: The Passage Body provides two key pieces of evidence: (1) both sTM and SOFA score individually have high predictive accuracy for 28-day mortality in HFRS (AUCs of 0.9317 and 0.9309, respectively), and (2) their combination yields a higher AUC (0.9492). By applying standard epidemiological reasoning—specifically, the interpretation of ROC curve analysis and AUC values—the conclusion that the combined model outperforms either marker alone is directly derivable. This conclusion is not explicitly stated in the Results section as a comparative claim but is logically inferred from the presented AUC values. It satisfies the novelty requirement because the comparative superiority of the combination is not directly asserted in the Results, and it meets the derivability and complexity requirements by integrating multiple data points and applying a standard statistical principle.

34.Option: Development based on Regional Rivalry, where there are high challenges to both mitigation and adaptation, could contribute to the highest proportional increase in dengue cases in the near term, while sustainability-focused development is projected to result in a relatively lesser increase due to improved health infrastructure.
34.Discussion_Source: We report that India is witnessing increased outbreaks and geographical expansions, especially in the malaria-endemic regions. We identified that urbanisation continues to be one of the primary drivers of the increased transmission; however, the rural areas should not be ignored, as a few states with higher rural populations have reported high cases. We also predict that the dengue cases will continue to increase, as indicated by the ensemble models, but the impact of socio-economic development will be different across the states. Our predictions show that development based on Regional Rivalry, where there are high challenges to both mitigation and adaptation, could contribute to the highest proportional increase in the near scenario. In contrast, the development focusing on Sustainability could witness a relatively lesser increase because of a concerted focus on health infrastructure.
Evidence: The projected changes in annual normalised cases for each state relative to 2022 and corresponding to different SSPs in 2030 are shown in Fig 7a. For the near scenario, i.e., in 2030, the relative changes could be differential across the states. We observe that the southern states of Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu are projected to have an increase between 10–80%, whereas the states of Kerala and Goa will have a relative decrease. In contrast, the western states of Gujarat and Maharashtra are expected to have the maximum proportional increase in 2030. This trend was also observed between 2016 and 2022 (Phase 2). These states are projected to experience significant urbanisation, population growth, and rising per-capita income [90,51].

In 2030, a development focused on SSP3 (1001.47; 95% CI: 620.23, 1382.72) is projected to have the highest normalised cases per 10 million, followed by SSP2 (978.24; 95% CI: 626.59, 1329.89). Both SSP1 (874.2; 95% CI: 535.4, 1212.9) and SSP5 (888.02; 95% CI: 521.2, 1254.9) have a relatively lesser burden.

Under the SSP1 mode of development, a maximum relative decrease and the minimum relative increase are projected for ~75% of the states. As discussed earlier, SSP5 is also leading to a relatively lesser increase and a higher decrease. Although development that follows an SSP3 scenario is going to witness the maximum burden, SSP1 or sustainability is the scenario that will see fewer outbreaks.
34.Rationale: The conclusion integrates multiple pieces of evidence from the Passage Body: (1) the ensemble model predicts higher dengue case burdens under SSP3 (Regional Rivalry) compared to SSP1 (Sustainability) in 2030; (2) SSP3 is associated with high challenges to mitigation and adaptation; (3) SSP1 is linked to improved health infrastructure and lower projected increases. These findings are derived from the model’s scenario-based projections and the interpretation of SSPs, which are explicitly defined in the Passage Body. The conclusion is not a direct numerical summary but a causal inference about the differential impact of socio-economic development pathways on dengue transmission, requiring integration of model outputs, scenario definitions, and epidemiological reasoning. It is novel (not stated directly in Results), derivable from the data and model, and complex, involving multiple variables and long-term projections.

35.Option: After accounting for diagnostic error and study-level uncertainty through misclassification-aware hierarchical modeling, exposure appears globally distributed but uneven, with higher levels concentrated near wildlife–livestock interfaces and in intensively monitored settings.
35.Discussion_Source: After accounting for diagnostic error and study-level uncertainty through misclassification-aware hierarchical modeling, exposure appears globally distributed but uneven, with higher levels concentrated near wildlife–livestock interfaces and in intensively monitored settings.
Evidence: Using a misclassification-aware model that integrates all serological assays performed on the same animals, we estimated the global true seroprevalence (θ) of Brucella exposure in wild canids. Across 48 wild populations (N = 3,925 animals), the N-weighted global true seroprevalence was 8.2% (95% CI: 5.1–11.3%).

In contrast, only a small number of cases were confirmed by PCR or culture (3.9%; 95% CI: 3.0–5.1%), probably reflecting both the rarity of true infection and differences in testing availability between regions.

Seroprevalence differed across continents in consistent and biologically plausible ways. Europe showed the lowest exposure (~0.8%), with most wolves, jackals, and arctic foxes seronegative, while older red-fox data accounted for isolated outliers. North America exhibited low-to-moderate exposure (~4.1%), consistent with localized transmission at livestock interfaces rather than broad enzootic circulation. South America had higher values (~18%), largely in fox species from agro-pastoral landscapes, though confirmatory data (0/40 PCR or culture) remain absent.

Species composition also contributed: synanthropic canids, particularly coyotes (Canis latrans), showed the highest weighted seroprevalence (~15.6%), likely due to frequent contact with livestock environments, feeding on infected tissues, and shared resource use in peri-urban or agricultural landscapes.

The hierarchical Bayesian models, which explicitly correct for imperfect sensitivity and specificity and share information across studies, produced higher global seroprevalence estimates (approximately 16–27%, centered around 21–23%), as expected under diagnostic uncertainty and high heterogeneity.
Posterior predictive checks, convergence diagnostics, and influence assessments all supported model stability, and robust or influence-trimmed variants yielded consistent results.
35.Rationale: The conclusion integrates multiple pieces of evidence from the Passage Body: (1) the initial seroprevalence estimate of 8.2% (95% CI: 5.1–11.3%) from a misclassification-aware model; (2) the regional variation in seroprevalence (lowest in Europe, higher in South America, moderate in North America); (3) the elevated seroprevalence in synanthropic species like coyotes linked to livestock contact; (4) the model's recalibration to 16–27% due to diagnostic uncertainty; and (5) the validation of model stability through convergence and predictive checks. The conclusion is not explicitly stated in the Passage Body but is logically derived by applying epidemiological principles—specifically, the correction for diagnostic misclassification and the interpretation of regional patterns in the context of ecological exposure. It reflects a key finding that exposure is not uniformly distributed but is concentrated where wildlife and livestock interact, a pattern revealed only after adjusting for methodological biases in the data. This conclusion meets the complexity, derivability, and novelty requirements.

36.Option: The combined suitability for JEV transmission was limited in broad continental terms by the minimum night time land surface temperatures that dominated the model of suitability for vectors and then constrained geographically by the strong proximity of ardeid host habitat to wetlands and areas subject to inundation.
36.Discussion_Source: The combined suitability for JEV transmission was limited in broad continental terms by the minimum night time land surface temperatures that dominated the model of suitability for vectors and then constrained geographically by the strong proximity of ardeid host habitat to wetlands and areas subject to inundation.
Evidence: Night time temperature was the most important covariate in the vector suitability models, and the most influential dynamic covariate in the models of ardeid habitat suitability, with temperatures below around 10–15 C associated with markedly lower suitability.
Ardeid habitat suitability was most strongly influenced by the cover of herbaceous wetland and areas frequently (though not permanently) subject to inundation where standing water becomes available.

The resulting spatial expression of predictions from the habitat suitability model for the selected Culex species was high suitability over large swathes of mainland Australia during the austral Summer of 2021/22 (December–February, Fig 1D and 1H, and see the full sequence of monthly predictions (S1 Animation in S1 File).
By winter (June 2022) suitability was restricted to areas at the tropical and equatorial latitudes (Fig 1H and 1I) due to the strong influence of night-time temperatures.
36.Rationale: The conclusion integrates two key findings from the Passage Body: (1) night-time temperature is the dominant factor limiting vector habitat suitability, with suitability dropping sharply below 10–15°C, and (2) ardeid host habitat suitability is strongly tied to wetlands and areas subject to inundation. The Passage Body further shows that vector suitability is high in tropical and sub-tropical regions during summer but declines sharply in winter due to temperature constraints, while ardeid habitat is concentrated in wetland-rich areas. The combined model, which takes the minimum of vector and host suitability at each location, therefore reflects a geographic limitation driven first by temperature (which restricts vector presence) and second by the spatial distribution of wetlands (which constrain host presence). This inference is not explicitly stated in the Passage Body but is logically derived from the interplay of these two environmental drivers and their spatial-temporal patterns, using standard epidemiological reasoning about transmission ecology and habitat suitability modeling.

37.Option: SIS supplementation alone is currently the best method for inducing the sexualization of liver flukes in vitro, as it enhances area increase, change in body shape, and reproductive organ development, whereas red blood cells do not induce changes in body shape and are potentially toxic to juveniles.
37.Discussion_Source: In this assay, some 11 dpi juveniles died with RBC, regardless of the presence or absence of the SIS combination, whereas no juveniles died with SIS alone, suggesting the toxicity of RBC to the juveniles. This speculation is supported by the observation of dead juveniles in all RBC-related assays in this study. Although the results of this study alone do not permit definitive conclusions, the toxicity of RBC may explain the elimination of this combined effect. One of the expected toxicities of RBC is oxidative stress caused by free iron derived from heme [37]. We speculated that the effects of SIS might be inhibited by oxidative stress; however, the detailed mechanism of this inhibition could not be investigated in this study. Anaerobic cultures without oxygen or antioxidant supplementation should be tested in the future to determine whether they can rescue juveniles from RBC-induced oxidative stress. For example, because ascorbic acid is supplemented in the in vitro culture of schistosomes [38,39], the medium composition can be improved by including antioxidants to prevent oxidative stress. Nevertheless, the results of this study showed that SIS supplementation alone is currently the best method for inducing the sexualization of liver flukes in vitro.
Evidence: In the culture of 11 dpi juveniles (Fig 4C), 1/4 juvenile with RBC died after 44 days of incubation, 1/4 juvenile was fixed at 91 days, and the remaining 2/4 juveniles were active until the endpoint of 98 days (S1 Movie, RBC group). In the basic medium, 1/4 juvenile was fixed at 91 days of incubation for comparison with RBC, and the remaining 3/4 juveniles survived until the endpoint.

In the combined incubation, the median body area increased to 1.17 mm2 and 1.68 mm2 in the 1 × SIS + RBC and 3 × SIS + RBC groups, respectively, which did not exceed the results of single supplementation of the SIS fractions (Fig 7B). The body area of 1 × SIS + RBC was smaller than that of 1 × SIS alone, with significant differences between 9 and 21 days of culture (Fig 7B), whereas no significant difference was observed between 3 × SIS and 3 × SIS + RBC (Fig 7B). The oral cone indices of 1 × SIS + RBC and 3 × SIS + RBC were smaller than those of the respective SIS fractions alone (Fig 7B).

In the RBC group, 1/16 juvenile died at 9 days of incubation, 1/16 juvenile died at 11 days, and 1/16 juvenile escaped at 16 days, and the remaining 13/16 juveniles survived until the endpoint. In the 1 × SIS + RBC group, 1/16 juvenile died at 4 days of incubation, and the remaining 15/16 juveniles survived until the endpoint. In the 3 × SIS + RBC group, 2/16 juveniles died at 4 days of incubation, 1/16 juvenile died at 7 days, 1/16 juvenile escaped at 7 days, 1/16 juvenile died at 11 days, 1/16 juvenile escaped at 14 days, and the remaining 10/16 juveniles survived until the endpoint.

In the culture of 11 dpi juveniles (Fig 5C), 1/4 juvenile was removed from both SIS and control groups and fixed at 91 days for comparative purposes. All remaining 3/4 juveniles survived and actively moved until the endpoint of 98 days (S1 Movie, SIS group).

SIS enhanced an increase in area, change in body shape, and reproductive organ development, although the last one was incomplete. In this assay, no concentration-dependency of SIS was observed. Consequently, it was speculated that SIS does not serve as a nutrient source but rather functions at low concentrations, inducing unknown biological changes that lead to the development of oral cones and testes.
37.Rationale: The conclusion is derived from multiple lines of evidence in the Passage Body: (1) SIS supplementation leads to significant increases in body area, changes in body shape (oral cone index), and testis development, while RBC does not induce body shape changes; (2) RBC supplementation is associated with juvenile deaths and reduced survival, especially in combination with SIS, suggesting toxicity; (3) the combined use of SIS and RBC does not improve outcomes and may even reduce them, indicating that RBC interferes with SIS effects; (4) SIS alone consistently produces positive developmental outcomes without mortality. These findings, when integrated using standard epidemiological and experimental reasoning, support the inference that SIS alone is superior and currently the best method for inducing sexualization in vitro, despite the incomplete maturation of reproductive organs. This conclusion is not explicitly stated in the Passage Body but is logically derived from the comparative data on survival, growth, and morphological development across conditions.

38.Option: The immunoregulation observed in A. ceylanicum may be a general phenomenon found in many other parasitic nematodes.
38.Discussion_Source: The immunoregulation we observe here for A. ceylanicum may be a general phenomenon found in many other parasitic nematodes.
Evidence: Immunoregulated genes of A. ceylanicum have orthologs in A. caninum, N. americanus, and H. contortus.
For the strongylid T. circumcincta, being embedded in host mucosa upregulates ES genes and putative immunomodulatory genes [92,184].
For the strongylid H. bakeri, infecting mouse hosts with colitis induces different ES proteins than normal hosts [198].

For the strongylid N. brasiliensis, recent transcriptomic and proteomic analyses shows genes that are positively or negatively regulated during infections of normal versus immunocompromised stat6 mutant mouse hosts, a subset of which encode ES proteins [52,199].
38.Rationale: The conclusion is derived from the integration of multiple lines of evidence from the Passage Body: (1) the presence of orthologous immunoregulated genes in other parasitic nematodes (A. caninum, N. americanus, H. contortus), suggesting evolutionary conservation; (2) independent findings in other strongylid nematodes (T. circumcincta, H. bakeri, N. brasiliensis) showing gene expression changes in response to host immune status or infection conditions, including upregulation of ES and immunomodulatory genes. These findings collectively support the inference that immunoregulation is not unique to A. ceylanicum but likely represents a broader, conserved mechanism across parasitic nematodes. The conclusion is not explicitly stated in the Passage Body but is logically derivable through epidemiological and comparative biological reasoning, and it meets the complexity requirement by synthesizing data across species and experimental models.

39.Option: High antigen-binding activity in vitro does not necessarily correlate with protective efficacy in vivo, underscoring the need to integrate both binding and functional assays when evaluating antibody performance.
39.Discussion_Source: Importantly, this outcome advances our understanding of antivenom development by demonstrating that high antigen-binding activity in vitro does not always correlate with protective efficacy in vivo, underscoring the need to integrate both binding and functional assays when evaluating antibody performance and to address the structural and mechanistic barriers in the design of next-generation recombinant antivenoms.
Evidence: Among the three constructs, the bispecific VHH-Fc exhibited the strongest antigen-binding response, followed by VHH-αNTX-Fc and VHH-PLA2-Fc.

In the murine model, VHH-αNTX-Fc conferred the greatest protection at an 2xLD₁₀₀ dose corresponding to 2.2xLD₅₀, yielding the highest survival rates, whereas the bispecific VHH-Fc showed only moderate protective efficacy.
This discrepancy underscores that strong in vitro binding is not necessarily predictive of therapeutic performance in vivo.
39.Rationale: The Passage Body provides two key sets of data: (1) in vitro binding results showing that the bispecific VHH-Fc had the strongest binding to crude N. kaouthia venom in ELISA, and (2) in vivo neutralization results showing that VHH-αNTX-Fc provided superior protection (highest survival rates) compared to the bispecific construct despite its lower binding affinity. This contrast between high in vitro binding and lower in vivo efficacy for the bispecific construct is explicitly highlighted in the Discussion as a key finding. The conclusion is derived by applying standard epidemiological and translational research principles: the disconnect between biomarker (binding) and clinical outcome (survival) indicates that in vitro assays alone are insufficient for predicting therapeutic success. This conclusion is not stated directly in the Passage Body but is logically inferable from the juxtaposition of the ELISA and survival data, and it meets all requirements: it is novel (not in Results), derivable from the data, complex (integrates multiple findings), and not speculative or generic.

40.Option: The persistence of neglected infectious diseases in quilombola communities of the Lower Amazon is strongly linked to structural conditions such as insufficient sanitation, inadequate water supply, precarious housing, and limitations in waste management, which reflect longstanding inequities and require integrated, territorially sensitive public policies for effective reduction.
40.Discussion_Source: The results of this study suggest that the persistence of NIDs in quilombola communities of the Lower Amazon is strongly linked to the structural conditions that shape everyday life, including insufficient sanitation, inadequate water supply, precarious housing, and limitations in waste management. These conditions reflect longstanding inequities and reveal vulnerabilities that may be mitigated through more consistent and territorially sensitive public policies.
Evidence: The absence of a bathroom in the household showed the strongest association (OR 5.87; 95%CI: 3.42–10.08).
The use of river water (OR 4.32; 95%CI: 2.15–8.67) and well water (OR 2.14; 95%CI: 1.08–4.24) were also relevant factors.
Poor housing conditions, characterized by dwellings not built with masonry, showed an OR of 4.12 (95%CI: 2.54–6.68).
Inadequate waste disposal increased the risk of NIDs (OR 3.45; 95%CI: 2.18–5.46).
Residing in a rural area (OR 2.89) and having a monthly family income of up to R$ 1,500.00 (OR 2.56) were also associated with the occurrence of NIDs.
The cluster characterized by multidimensional poverty showed the highest prevalence of NIDs (52.3%), followed by the sanitary vulnerability cluster (41.7%).
Communities such as Tiningu and Arapemã are classified in the highest risk category, while Pérola do Maicá and Saracura present lower relative risk levels.

The territorial risk map highlights the spatial inequality that permeates the Lower Amazon. Communities located farther from urban centers, such as Tiningu and Arapemã, exhibited critical risk levels, consistent with research on geographic access showing that long distances, lack of regular transportation, and river seasonality significantly increase barriers to care.
40.Rationale: The conclusion integrates multiple lines of evidence from the Passage Body: (1) multivariate regression results showing strong, independent associations between NIDs and key socioenvironmental factors (lack of bathroom, unsafe water, poor housing, inadequate waste disposal); (2) cluster analysis revealing that multidimensional poverty and sanitary vulnerability are linked to the highest disease prevalence; and (3) spatial analysis demonstrating that remote, geographically isolated communities have the highest risk levels. These findings collectively support the inference that NIDs are not merely the result of individual risk behaviors but are deeply embedded in structural, spatial, and historical inequities. The conclusion is not explicitly stated in the Passage Body but is logically derived by synthesizing statistical associations, cluster patterns, and spatial distribution data, applying epidemiological principles of social determinants of health and health equity. It meets the novelty, derivability, and complexity requirements by integrating data across multiple analytical methods and levels of analysis.

41.Option: The proposed 5D Healing Framework offers a roadmap for practice, research, and policy that prioritizes dignity, resilience, and inclusion as much as medical outcomes in leprosy care.
41.Discussion_Source: This review demonstrates that achieving zero leprosy requires care that transcends bacteriological cure, embracing mental, social, economic, and spiritual dimensions alongside the biomedical. By drawing lessons from HIV, TB, diabetes, and mental health, and adapting them thoughtfully, leprosy programs can move toward genuinely holistic, person-centered care. The proposed framework offers a roadmap for practice, research, and policy—one that prioritizes dignity, resilience, and inclusion as much as medical outcomes.
Evidence: Despite these long-term consequences, individuals are declared ‘cured’ once MDT is completed, in line with the current biomedical definition of cure. However, for them, cure extends beyond bacteriological clearance to encompass the ability to return to pre disease conditions, daily activities, work, family, and social life.
Current treatment pathways do not have mechanisms to address these, resulting in many who do not feel fully healed and are left stranded in their journey toward restoration.
The voices of Persons living with HIV/AIDs have been vocal and have played an important role in reshaping attitudes of the public and within the care providers in the health services.
WHO frameworks on disability-inclusive development further reinforce the need to address long-term functioning, participation, and dignity beyond disease-specific treatment.
This review provides evidence from HIV, TB, diabetes, and schizophrenia but differences in stigma, chronicity, and programmatic infrastructure mean that transferability cannot be assumed.

For research, priorities include testing care packages in leprosy contexts, using robust designs to evaluate feasibility to embed them in public health programs, their effectiveness and lived experiences.
41.Rationale: The Passage Body establishes that leprosy treatment ends with bacteriological cure (MDT completion), but individuals continue to face disability, stigma, psychological distress, and socioeconomic challenges long after treatment. It emphasizes that current care pathways fail to address these ongoing needs, leaving patients feeling unhealed. The text draws parallels with HIV, TB, diabetes, and schizophrenia, where holistic, person-centered care models have been developed to address psychological, social, economic, and spiritual dimensions. The Discussion explicitly states that the 5D Healing Framework integrates these dimensions and serves as a roadmap for practice, research, and policy. This conclusion is derivable from the evidence: the persistent suffering post-cure, the success of similar models in other diseases, and the call for integrated, rights-based care. It is not directly stated in the Passage Body, requires integration of multiple pieces of evidence, and reflects a key, complex inference about the future direction of leprosy care.

42.Option: The 1.4% seroprevalence of RVF virus among febrile patients in the DRC cohort, despite no documented human cases, indicates low but existing exposure to the virus, suggesting potential underdiagnosis or underreporting in the country.
42.Discussion_Source: The 1.4% seroprevalence of RVF virus among febrile patients in the DRC cohort, despite no documented human cases, indicates low but existing exposure. This suggests potential underdiagnosis or underreporting in the country.
Evidence: A total of 253 participants (5.3%) tested positive for RVF by serology and/or molecular testing with a significant difference between countries with 19/1370 (1.4%) subjects in DRC, 29/1468 (2.0%) subjects in Kenya and 205/1,968 (10.4%) subjects in Uganda, p < 0.001 (Table 1).

Apart from an article published in 1999, identifying RVF virus IgG antibodies in two Kisangani residents, in the central-eastern part of the DRC, to the best of our knowledge no other reports exist [33] and no RVF virus-related hemorrhagic fever events have been documented in humans to date.

In particular, in the North Kivu, Goma region, a 2013 study reported 12.7% RVF IgG prevalence and 2.0% RVF IgM prevalence in cattle, indicating the presence of a potential recent/silent circulation [19].
Taken together, these data suggest a potentially inadequate RVF surveillance system with possible underdiagnosis and/or underreporting, especially for milder cases that may go undetected.
42.Rationale: The Passage Body provides three key pieces of evidence: (1) 1.4% of febrile patients in the DRC tested positive for RVF (seropositivity), (2) no human RVF cases have been documented in the DRC to date, and (3) prior evidence of RVF virus circulation in animals (cattle) in the same region. By applying standard epidemiological reasoning—specifically, interpreting seroprevalence in the absence of reported cases as indicative of undetected transmission—the conclusion that there is low but existing exposure, likely due to underdiagnosis or underreporting, is logically derived. This conclusion is not explicitly stated in the Passage Body but is a direct inference from the combination of seroprevalence data, lack of case documentation, and evidence of animal circulation. It meets the novelty, derivability, and complexity requirements, as it integrates multiple data points across human and animal health and applies general principles of surveillance gaps and silent transmission.

43.Option: The maps provide a baseline to guide surveillance, entomological studies, and ecological investigations in data-limited regions, despite the complex, multi-host and multi-vector transmission systems of most zoonotic arboviruses.
43.Discussion_Source: These outputs should be interpreted as screening tools rather than predictors of disease occurrence. Given the complex, multi-host and multi-vector transmission systems of most zoonotic arboviruses, the maps provide a baseline to guide surveillance, entomological studies, and ecological investigations in data-limited regions.
Evidence: We modeled habitat suitability for three viruses (WSLV, SINV, and MIDV) and five mosquito vectors (Ae. circumluteolus, Ae. mcintoshi, Cx. univittatus, Cx. pipiens and Ma. africana).

Our models predict that most SSA countries show variable suitability for the analyzed mosquito species, a finding consistent with mosquito collections since the 1970s which identified arbovirus vectors in multiple countries [42,51].

The vectors we analyzed are also important vectors for other viruses of public health importance, i.e., Ae. circumluteolus (Spondweni, Zika, Lebombo, Kedougou, Bunyamwera, Ndumu, Pongola and RVF); Ae. mcintoshi (Babanki, Ndumu, Bunyamwera, Ngari, Pongola, RVF); Cx. univittatus (West Nile, Usutu, WSLV, RVF); Cx. pipiens (West Nile, Usutu, Semliki Forest, RVF, Japanese Encephalitis, Venezuelan Equine Encephalitis), Ma. africana (Spondweni, Usutu, RVF) [4,95,96].
Many viral pathogens in this study are not notifiable or routinely monitored, limiting case data from many African countries.
Despite these challenges, we are confident that we compiled a representative dataset from surveillance, outbreaks, and research, incorporating diverse diagnostic methods and reputable sources.

Arboviral transmission depends on complex and dynamic processes—including vector–host interactions, vector competence, pathogen prevalence, immunity, and human mobility—that cannot be fully captured using presence-only ecological models.
43.Rationale: The conclusion is derived from the integration of multiple pieces of evidence: (1) the study models ecological suitability for three neglected arboviruses and five mosquito vectors across Africa using presence-only data; (2) the authors acknowledge that the viruses are not routinely monitored and that data are sparse; (3) the transmission systems are complex and multi-host, with limited understanding of vector competence and host dynamics; (4) the models are explicitly described as not predicting actual disease transmission but rather ecological suitability. From these, the logical inference is that despite the limitations, the maps serve as a foundational tool to guide future research and surveillance in data-poor regions. This conclusion is not directly stated in the Passage Body but is a necessary inference based on the study’s methodology, limitations, and stated purpose, and it meets the complexity, derivability, and novelty requirements.

44.Option: The SARS-CoV-2 pandemic may have promoted the evolution of HCoV-OC43, with adaptive mutations in the spike and nucleocapsid proteins enhancing viral ability to recognize and bind to host sialic acid receptors, facilitating membrane fusion and viral assembly, and promoting efficient host cell entry.
44.Discussion_Source: The SARS-CoV-OC43 pandemic may have promoted the evolution of HCoV-OC43. Under selection pressure, adaptive mutations at key amino acid sites in the spike and nucleocapsid proteins of HCoV-OC43 may enhance the virus’s ability to recognize and bind to host sialic acid receptors, facilitate membrane fusion and viral assembly, and promote efficient host cell entry.
Evidence: The spike protein of coronaviruses is known for its high variability and frequent mutations [14,32,33], whereas the RdRp and N proteins are relatively conserved [14,32].
In genotype K, we observed that the S gene exhibited the highest nucleotide substitution rate, whereas the RdRp gene showed the slowest.

For genotype K, which currently occupies a dominant position after the emergence of SARS-CoV-2, the overall nucleotide substitution rate at the WG level was estimated at 2.2156 × 10 ⁻ ⁴ nucleotide substitutions/site/year (95% HPD: 1.7252 × 10 ⁻ ⁴, 2.7172 × 10 ⁻ ⁴), and the time to the most recent common ancestor (tMRCA) traced to approximately mid-June 2010 (2010.4476; 95% HPD: 2002.1353, 2015.0588) (S2 Table).

Comparison of total nucleotide substitution rates across the S, RdRp, and N genes revealed that the S gene exhibited the highest rate, whereas the RdRp gene showed the slowest (S2 Table and Fig 2A-2D).

Furthermore, by comparing the nucleotide substitution rates of the WG, S, RdRp, and N genes before and after the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic, there was an accelerated evolutionary trend in all four genetic levels. The acceleration was most pronounced in the S gene, with nucleotide substitution rates increasing from 2.3757 × 10 ⁻ ⁴ (95% HPD: 9.4851 × 10 ⁻ ⁵, 3.9034 × 10 ⁻ ⁴) to 8.9403 × 10 ⁻ ⁴ (95% HPD: 4.9075 × 10 ⁻ ⁴, 1.3053 × 10 ⁻ ³) (S2 Table and Fig 2A-2D).

Positively selected sites were found only in the S and N proteins of genotype K (behaving as genotype I at the N gene level) and in the S protein of genotype J (S3 Table). Specifically, seventeen positively selected sites (identified by at least one method) were detected in the S protein of genotype K: twelve—sites 25, 26, 38, 40, 67, 89, 195, 199, 265, 266, 270, and 271—were located in the N-terminal domain (NTD) of the S1 subunit; two—sites 504 and 506—were in the C-terminal domain (CTD) of the S1 subunit; one—site 900—was in the fusion peptide (FP) region of the S2 subunit; two—sites 1251 and 1338—were in the other region (site 1251 was mapped to the stem helix region) of the S protein (S3 Table). In the N protein of genotype K, three positively selected sites were identified at sites 49, 79, and 248 (S3 Table).

Of the positively selected sites identified in the S protein of genotype K, sites 38 (33) and 40 (35) are situated near the binding region, whereas site 89 (84) resides directly within it, suggesting potential functional relevance (S3C Fig).

The results of historical evolution analysis showed that amino acid mutations at positively selected sites almost all occurred along internal nodes of the time-scaled maximum clade credibility (MCC) trees. Lots of mutations at positively selected sites in genotype K, including R26G/T, P38L/S, S40P, L67V, S265A, S270N, L271S, and D1251A, were observed at tree nodes or within subclades corresponding to sequences collected after the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic.

In genotype K, the accumulation of adaptive mutations at multiple positively selected sites in the S1 NTD, S2 fusion peptide region, and N protein, along with possible co-evolution among these regions (NTD-FP-N), may enhance the viral ability to recognize and bind to host cell sialic acid receptors, improve membrane fusion and viral replication/assembly efficiency, and ultimately facilitate more efficient host cell entry and transmission.
44.Rationale: The conclusion is derived from multiple lines of evidence in the Passage Body: (1) the S gene of HCoV-OC43, particularly in the dominant genotype K, shows a significant increase in nucleotide substitution rates post-pandemic, indicating accelerated evolution; (2) positively selected sites—indicating adaptive evolution—are concentrated in the S protein (especially in the NTD and fusion peptide) and the N protein of genotype K; (3) several of these sites (e.g., 89, 38, 40) are located in or near the receptor-binding region of the spike protein; (4) these mutations are predominantly observed in post-pandemic sequences, suggesting they emerged under recent selective pressure. By applying standard epidemiological and evolutionary principles—interpreting substitution rate increases as evidence of accelerated evolution, positively selected sites as markers of adaptive change, and spatial clustering of mutations in functional domains as evidence of functional impact—the conclusion that the pandemic drove adaptive evolution enhancing host cell entry is logically and directly inferable. This conclusion is not explicitly stated in the Passage Body but is a synthesis of multiple findings, satisfying the novelty, derivability, and complexity requirements.

45.Option: The lack of standardized vital statistics in high-burden Low- and Middle-Income Countries (LMICs) is likely a major driver of substantial underestimation of HEV mortality.
45.Discussion_Source: While global mortality estimates vary significantly, the lack of standardized vital statistics in high-burden Low- and Middle-Income Countries (LMICs) is likely a major driver of substantial underestimation.
Evidence: In GBD 2019 countries such as India, Bangladesh, and Nepal, with a very large burden of disease, did not contribute any sources to these death estimates.

Deaths occurring in outbreaks, particularly in camps for displaced people, are not captured in any national vital statistics as it is often unclear which government is responsible for recording the information.
The number of HE cases and HEV infections is also difficult to estimate due to poor surveillance and lack of reporting.

There are only 8 sources from Africa and 34 from Asia, yet most of those are from East and Central Asia. There are 28 sources from European countries despite a smaller burden of disease in Europe compared to Southeast Asia and Africa (Table 4).
45.Rationale: The Passage Body establishes that high-burden countries like India, Bangladesh, and Nepal—despite having large HEV burdens—did not contribute data to global mortality estimates. It further explains that outbreak-related deaths in displaced populations are not captured in national vital statistics due to jurisdictional ambiguity. The evidence also shows a stark imbalance in data availability: Europe has more published sources than Africa and Asia combined, despite the latter regions bearing the highest burden. These facts, when combined with the epidemiological principle that mortality estimates depend on reliable reporting systems, allow the logical inference that the absence of standardized vital statistics in LMICs is a key reason for underestimation. This conclusion is not explicitly stated in the Passage Body but is derivable from the integration of multiple pieces of evidence about data gaps, reporting failures, and geographic disparities in data availability.

46.Option: The observed downward trend in cystic echinococcosis hospitalisations in Italy is primarily driven by a steady decrease in case numbers rather than changes in treatment type, and the abrupt decline in 2020 was likely due to disruptions caused by the COVID-19 pandemic rather than a true epidemiological shift.
46.Discussion_Source: The observed downward trend in costs was primarily driven by a steady decrease in the hospitalisation numbers, rather than by any significant changes in treatment type (surgical or medical) that could account for the reduction in expenses. On the other hand, despite the increase of reimbursements by the Italian National Health Service in 2013, the average annual economic burden of CE decreased by almost 3-fold, from €6,398 per 100,000 inhabitants (2001–2014) to €2,243 per 100,000 inhabitants (2015–2022) [9]. The abrupt decline in 2020 coincided with the COVID-19 pandemic, when routine healthcare access was disrupted. This phenomenon has also been noted in other neglected diseases, where diagnosis and treatment were deprioritized during the health emergency, mainly in middle and low income countries [34]. The rebound to pre-pandemic trends in subsequent years indicates that the decline was artificial rather than epidemiological.
Evidence: During the period covered in this study, CE trend, in Italy, (Fig 4) appeared to be decreasing from 2015 to 2022. The number of Italian patients decreased gradually and steadily from 326 in 2015–165 in 2022. However, there was an abrupt drop in 2020 when the national health system’s focus was almost entirely on solving the emergency caused by the COVID-19 pandemic.

The proportions of surgical and medical treatments in patients hospitalised for CE remained stable during the study period, except for the year 2022, when surgery rates increased compared to medical therapy.
The rebound to pre-pandemic trends in subsequent years indicates that the decline was artificial rather than epidemiological.
46.Rationale: The Passage Body provides data on the steady decline in CE hospitalisations from 326 cases in 2015 to 165 in 2022, with an abrupt drop in 2020. It also states that treatment proportions (surgical vs. medical) remained stable over time, except for a minor change in 2022. This indicates that the reduction in hospitalisations—and thus in costs—was not due to changes in treatment patterns. The Discussion explicitly links the 2020 drop to the disruption caused by the COVID-19 pandemic and notes that the trend rebounded afterward, suggesting the decline was not epidemiological but due to healthcare system strain. This conclusion integrates the temporal pattern of hospitalisations, the stability of treatment types, and the contextual event of the pandemic, making it a logically derived, non-redundant, and complex inference not directly stated in the Passage Body.

47.Option: PS was observed in 5% of women without detectable S. haematobium eggs in urine, suggesting that placental schistosomiasis could be an underestimated phenomenon in highly endemic regions and warrants further investigation into its implications for mother-and-child health.
47.Discussion_Source: Notably, PS was also observed in 5% of women without detectable S. haematobium eggs in urine. This suggests that PS could be an underestimated phenomenon in highly endemic regions and warrants further investigations of its implications for mother-and-child health.
Evidence: Among infected women with available placental samples, the prevalence of PS was 14.3% (4/28; 95% CI: 4.0-32.7%), whereas among the women from the non-infected, control group with available placental samples the prevalence of PS was 5% (1/20; 95% CI: 0.1-24.9%).
All placental samples of women with detectable PS showed concordant qPCR results.
For one sample, the whole diagnostic pellet was used in light microscopy, so there was insufficient material for qPCR assessment.
47.Rationale: The Passage Body reports that PS was detected in 1 out of 20 (5%) women who tested negative for S. haematobium eggs in urine via light microscopy. This finding is supported by confirmatory qPCR in all other positive cases, indicating that the detection was not due to false-negative urine testing alone. The presence of PS in women with no detectable eggs in urine—despite the use of a sensitive maceration technique—suggests that placental involvement may occur independently of detectable maternal urinary infection. This conclusion is not explicitly stated in the Passage Body but is logically derived from the data: the co-occurrence of PS in a non-infected group, combined with molecular confirmation, implies that current diagnostic methods may miss cases of PS, especially when relying solely on urine microscopy. The inference that PS is underrecognized and warrants further study is directly supported by the evidence and aligns with the epidemiological principle that a disease manifestation can exist without detectable primary infection in standard diagnostic samples.

48.Option: The infectious nature of HAM/TSP, combined with low social awareness, necessitates unique self-management strategies that include managing the risk of transmission to close relatives and addressing the social stigma associated with the disease.
48.Discussion_Source: The infectious nature of HAM/TSP affects the self-management strategies. Individuals with HAM/TSP must consider the effects of HTLV-1 not only on themselves but also on their close relatives. This self-management strategy is specific to people with HAM/TSP and is not found in other neurological disorders. ... HAM/TSP is prone to social stigma owing to low social awareness of the disease and the fact that it is an infectious disease; thus, self-management strategies are required to minimize this impact.
Evidence: HAM/TSP is an infectious disease, and it can manifest with diverse symptoms.
The results of the present study identified as a category of “Concern about the impact of HTLV-1 infection on close relatives” within the core category “Taking control of HAM/TSP.”
HAM/TSP is prone to social stigma owing to low social awareness of the disease and the fact that it is an infectious disease; thus, self-management strategies are required to minimize this impact.

Davoudi et al. found that people with HAM/TSP, when they came to know of their HTLV-1 infection, experienced an impact on their desirable personal and social lives, as the fear of spreading the virus prevents them from continuing their marital lives and may even lead to divorce.

Zihlmann et al. found that many of their HTLV-1-infected participants tended to believe that their disease was an HIV infection or were in denial that they had HTLV-1, and that fear of exposing their infection and the destruction of family relationships that a diagnosis of HTLV-1 might cause led them to treat their diagnosis as a “secret”.
48.Rationale: The Passage Body establishes that HAM/TSP is an infectious disease caused by HTLV-1, which is transmitted through breastfeeding, sexual intercourse, blood transfusion, and needle sharing. It also states that the disease is poorly recognized socially, leading to stigma and misunderstanding. The study participants reported specific self-management behaviors, such as informing relatives about HTLV-1 status and avoiding transmission through intimate contact, which are directly tied to the disease’s infectious nature. Additionally, the text notes that fear of stigma leads to secrecy and social withdrawal. The Discussion explicitly links the infectious nature and low social awareness to the development of unique self-management strategies, including managing transmission risk and coping with stigma. This conclusion integrates multiple pieces of evidence from the Passage Body—disease transmission routes, social stigma, patient-reported behaviors, and the psychological impact of diagnosis—and applies epidemiological reasoning about how infectiousness and public perception shape health behaviors in chronic conditions. It is not a direct restatement of any single sentence but a logical inference derived from the data.

49.Option: The failure of exogenous serotonin to rescue motility in juveniles with silenced 5HT7 receptors indicates that these receptors are essential for mediating serotonin's stimulatory effects on motility in juvenile F. hepatica.
49.Discussion_Source: The reduced motility observed following 5HT₁ knockdown could reflect broader or indirect physiological roles, rather than direct mediation of acute serotonergic excitation. Although 5HT₁ receptors clearly contribute to motility regulation, their role may be more context-dependent. In vertebrates, 5HT₁ receptors are commonly Gi/o-coupled and involved in diverse modulatory functions within neural circuits [46,65]; whether comparable signaling roles operate in parasitic flatworms remains to be determined.[65] The reduced motility observed following 5HT₁ knockdown could reflect broader or indirect physiological roles, rather than direct mediation of acute serotonergic excitation. Although 5HT₁ receptors clearly contribute to motility regulation, their role may be more context-dependent. In vertebrates, 5HT₁ receptors are commonly Gi/o-coupled and involved in diverse modulatory functions within neural circuits [46,65]; whether comparable signaling roles operate in parasitic flatworms remains to be determined.[65]
Evidence: Exogenous 5-HT was applied to FhTPH-silenced juveniles. Exposure to 1 mM 5-HT for 18 hours restored and enhanced motility of FhTPH-silenced juveniles by tenfold, confirming that the phenotype reflects impaired serotonin availability rather than irreversible dysfunction (Fig 5D).

In contrast, no rescue was observed in juveniles with silenced 5HT7 receptors (Fig 5E), despite clear RNAi-induced motility deficits. Although knockdown of both 5HT₁ and 5HT7 receptors significantly reduced motility in the initial receptor RNAi experiment (Fig 5C), the failure of exogenous 5-HT to restore movement following 5HT7 silencing provides strong functional evidence that 5HT7 receptors are required for the enhanced motility effects of serotonin under the conditions tested.
49.Rationale: The Passage Body provides two key experimental findings: (1) exogenous serotonin fully rescues motility defects caused by silencing the serotonin synthesis enzyme FhTPH, confirming that the motility defect is due to lack of serotonin and not irreversible damage; and (2) when 5HT7 receptors are silenced, exogenous serotonin fails to restore motility, despite the presence of functional serotonin synthesis and release pathways. This differential rescue outcome—where serotonin rescues FhTPH knockdown but not 5HT7 receptor knockdown—logically implies that 5HT7 receptors are essential for mediating serotonin's stimulatory effect on motility. This conclusion is not explicitly stated in the Passage Body but is directly inferable from the experimental design and results. It requires integrating data from multiple figures (Fig 5D and 5E), applying the principle of functional rescue as a test of receptor necessity, and recognizing that a failure to rescue indicates a non-redundant, essential role for the targeted receptor. The conclusion is novel (not stated in the Passage Body), derivable from the evidence, and complex, requiring integration of multiple experimental outcomes.

50.Option: The observed increase in the spatial scale of onchocerciasis prevalence over time, expanding from approximately 32 km to about 180 km, suggests that transmission dynamics have become more diffuse, likely due to climate change and human migration, posing challenges to elimination efforts that traditionally target localized endemic foci.
50.Discussion_Source: The geostatistical analysis revealed a significant increase in the spatial scale of onchocerciasis prevalence over time, expanding from approximately 32 km (1997–2000) to about 180 km in more recent years (i.e., for any prediction location, its estimated value is influenced by locations up to 180 km away). Although this range is still within the long-distance flight capacity of the vectors (Simulium spp.) [48], the widening spatial scale appears plausible, as a study from Nigeria reported a prevalence of up to 26.4% in a local government area previously considered non-endemic for onchocerciasis [4,49]. This trend may be attributed to a combination of ecological and anthropogenic factors, particularly the effects of climate change and human migration [50]. Climate change can expand suitable habitats for Simulium blackflies by altering temperature and rainfall patterns, leading to the emergence of new breeding sites in areas that were previously non-endemic [51,52]. Simultaneously, increasing human mobility—driven by conflict, economic hardship, and climate-induced displacement—facilitates the movement of infected individuals into new regions, potentially introducing or reintroducing transmission in areas that were either non-endemic or had previously achieved control, respectively [53–55]. These dynamics may contribute to a broader and more diffuse pattern of transmission, posing challenges to elimination efforts that traditionally target localized endemic foci.

Increasing human mobility—driven by conflict, economic hardship, and climate-induced displacement—facilitates the movement of infected individuals into new regions, potentially introducing or reintroducing transmission in areas that were either non-endemic or had previously achieved control, respectively.
These dynamics may contribute to a broader and more diffuse pattern of transmission, posing challenges to elimination efforts that traditionally target localized endemic foci.

The conclusion integrates multiple pieces of evidence: the temporal change in spatial correlation, the biological plausibility of vector range expansion due to climate, and the epidemiological logic of human mobility spreading infection. It is not a direct restatement of a result, nor is it a limitation or future direction. It is a novel, logically derived inference about changing transmission dynamics, satisfying all requirements.

53.Discussion_Source: Our findings support the argument that public health technologies such as drones cannot be detached from the social systems in which they operate. Governance, or how drones are rolled out due to social and political processes, involves many relevant stakeholders that navigate complex settings and follow their own agendas. Project designers must prioritize clarity, co-design strategies, feedback mechanisms, and ethical safeguards for sustained implementation.
Evidence: The community’s characterization of dengue as a chronic, recurring burden rather than an episodic threat offers an important context for understanding their receptiveness to new technologies.

Participants repeatedly emphasized that the success of drone surveillance hinges on strategic deployment. They expect the drones to serve precise purposes, such as targeting difficult-to-access areas or hotspots identified by case clustering rather than random or symbolic flights.
When community members observe well-coordinated, data-driven deployment of drones, it reinforces trust in the broader intervention. On the contrary, repetitive or unfocused use can fuel skepticism.

Despite scholarship associating surveillance technologies with loss of privacy or intrusion [34], this study reveals that when drones are clearly positioned as tools for environmental monitoring, communities can distinguish them from forms of surveillance that feel threatening.

Material incentives did not primarily drive participation in the drone initiative. Instead, respondents expressed strong communal motivations. When projects are grounded in the local community’s values, many community members will see their involvement as part of a shared responsibility for safeguarding vulnerable children, the elderly, and those with pre-existing health conditions [35].
Being part of a public health innovation generated a sense of civic pride. People wanted to be seen as proactive contributors to national or global challenges.
53.Rationale: The conclusion integrates multiple strands of evidence from the Passage Body: (1) the community views dengue as a persistent, collective threat; (2) they expect drones to be deployed strategically and efficiently, not randomly; (3) trust is built through transparent communication and clear purpose; (4) privacy concerns are mitigated when drones are framed as environmental monitors, not personal surveillance; and (5) participation is driven by collective responsibility and civic pride, not material incentives. These elements are not explicitly stated as a single conclusion in the Passage Body but are logically derived by applying epidemiological principles of community engagement, behavioral motivation, and technology adoption in public health. The conclusion is novel (not directly stated), derivable from the evidence, complex (integrates social, technical, and behavioral dimensions), and avoids speculation or limitations.

59.Option: Coinfection with Plasmodium yoelii enhances the fecundity and within-host persistence of Heligmosomoides polygyrus, resulting in higher cumulative egg excretion in coinfected hosts compared to single-infected hosts, despite the absence of a trade-off between early and late reproductive investment.

If these results can be extrapolated to other systems involving human microparasites and STHs, they suggest that, in addition to the direct benefit for the host, targeting the coinfecting microparasites might also indirectly reduce helminth transmission success by reducing the number of transmissible stages found in the external environment and, consequently, reducing the risk of infection. 59.Rationale: The conclusion integrates multiple pieces of evidence from the Passage Body: (1) coinfection with Py increases fecundity (higher egg shedding) in Hp-infected mice, especially when Py infection occurs during the acute phase; (2) this increase is not transitory, as coinfected hosts excrete more eggs over the long term; (3) worms in coinfected hosts persist longer in the host, leading to a longer patent period; and (4) even when host mortality limits persistence in one scenario, cumulative egg excretion remains higher in coinfected hosts. Therefore, we propose that this peptide could serve as a valuable candidate for the development of new therapeutic agents to improve chemotherapy for Chagas disease.
Evidence: Cm-p5 significantly diminished the infected cells by 75% (Fig 6A) and the number of parasites per cell by 64.3% (Fig 6B) which reduced the infection index by 91.1% (Fig 6C).

This conclusion is not stated directly in the Passage Body but is logically derived from the combination of high sensitivity and moderate DICE score, along with the acknowledged limitations of the dataset and preprocessing. It meets the novelty, derivability, and complexity requirements by integrating multiple pieces of evidence and applying epidemiological and methodological reasoning about diagnostic tool design in resource-limited contexts.

94.Option: All partially clotted 20WBCT results, whether minimally or mostly clotted, should be interpreted as clotted and not indicative of the need for antivenom, based on the lack of significant differences in fibrinogen concentrations between these subcategories.
94.Discussion_Source: We suggest that clinicians interpret all partially clotted 20WBCT samples, whether major or minor, as if they were completely clotted.
Evidence: There were no significant differences among the completely clotted, mostly clotted, and minimally clotted groups, as illustrated in the dot plot (Fig 1).

In the completely clotted samples, 5.4% (3/56) had fibrinogen concentrations less than 100 mg/dL (82.9, 93.7, and 96.3 mg/dL). For the samples having major clot, 5 out of 112 samples (4.5%) revealed fibrinogen concentrations below 100 mg/dL (81.9, 83.3, 85.7, 93.9, and 99.7 mg/dL). In the samples with minor clot, 13.3% (2/15) had low fibrinogen concentrations (77.0 and 90.6 mg/dL).
We suggest that clinicians interpret all partially clotted 20WBCT samples, whether major or minor, as if they were completely clotted.
94.Rationale: The Passage Body shows that fibrinogen concentrations did not differ significantly between the completely clotted, mostly clotted, and minimally clotted 20WBCT groups. Furthermore, the proportion of samples with fibrinogen <100 mg/dL was low across all clotting states, including partially clotted samples. Since the clinical decision to administer antivenom is based on the presence of hypofibrinogenemia (fibrinogen <100 mg/dL), and since partially clotted samples do not show a meaningful difference in fibrinogen levels compared to completely clotted samples, it follows that all partially clotted results should be interpreted as normal (clotted) and not warrant antivenom. This conclusion is derived from the statistical equivalence of fibrinogen levels across clotting states and the low rate of hypofibrinogenemia in partially clotted samples, which supports a unified clinical interpretation.

95.Option: The detection of a novel Treponema species (Treponema sp. A) in the oral microbiomes of noma participants from two independent studies, using different metagenomic techniques, and its apparent very low frequency in healthy oral microbiomes, suggests that Treponema A may be associated with the development of noma.
95.Discussion_Source: Notably, we identified an uncultured, novel Treponema species (Treponema A) with high confidence from the majority (15/19) of noma patients in this study (Fig 4). Examination of the phylogeny of this novel species reveals it is more closely related to Treponema socranskii, a species frequently associated with severe periodontal tissue destruction [61], than it is to other known oral treponemes. Examination of previous 16S rRNA noma and associated ANG metagenomes also revealed the presence of Treponema sp. A in the majority of lesions sampled from participants with noma and ANG, while it was detected at very low frequency in the oral cavity of age matched control metagenomes in the same study [20]. The detection of this specific, novel treponeme in the oral metagenomes of noma participants from two independent studies, using different metagenomic techniques, and its apparent very low frequency in healthy oral microbiomes, suggests that Treponema A may be associated with the development of noma.
Evidence: Treponema sp. A was not detected in the participant with Stage 1 disease, nor the two participants with Stage 4 disease (scarring).

Through a combination of MAG and 16S rRNA gene recovery, we therefore detected Treponema sp. A in 15/19 noma participants assessed in this study, including 90% (8/9) of Stage 2 participants with oedema, and 100% (7/7) of Stage 3 participants with gangrenous lesions (S5 Table).

If 99% identity between 16S rRNA gene fragments was considered as a same species hit, Treponema sp. A was detected in 2/12 (16.7%), 10/12 (83.3%) and 7/12 (58.3%) of healthy, Stage 1 noma and established noma samples, respectively. Chi-square testing confirmed significant differences between the groups (p = 0.004).
Neither Treponema sp. A MAGs nor 16S rRNA genes were recoverable from the 20 metagenomes in the healthy global saliva dataset.
95.Rationale: The conclusion is derived from multiple lines of evidence in the Passage Body: (1) Treponema sp. A was detected in 15 out of 19 noma participants, with a strong association to more advanced disease stages (Stage 2 and 3); (2) it was absent in the only Stage 1 and two Stage 4 participants; (3) it was detected in a prior independent study using different methods (16S rRNA) and in a different cohort; (4) it was found at very low frequency in healthy controls in both the current and prior studies; and (5) it was not detected in the global healthy saliva dataset. These findings collectively support a strong association between Treponema sp. A and noma, particularly in the active disease phase, and not merely a random or background presence. The conclusion is not explicitly stated in the Passage Body but is logically inferable from the data using epidemiological reasoning about microbial associations and disease progression.
